warmup.q: Back to the shared card. Your payment was saved, and your phone was told OK. A moment later, your sister's phone read the balance from another copy and got the old 100.00. Which statement is true?
options: The system is broken: a system that keeps copies must never do this
It breaks the strictest promise, that the copies act like one, but it can still keep a looser promise
It breaks even the loosest promise, that the copies end up the same once the changes stop
It couldn't happen if every computer's clock showed exactly the same time
warmup.why: The strictest promise, called linearizable, says the copies must act like one: a read that starts after a write has finished must see it, and this one didn't. A looser promise, sequential consistency, only asks for one order that keeps each client's own steps in the order it took them. Putting your sister's read before your payment breaks nobody's order, so it allows this. The loosest promise, eventual consistency, says nothing about a single read, only that the copies agree once writes stop, and a moment later they did. Perfect clocks wouldn't help: her phone asked a copy that hadn't received the payment yet, and no clock can tell a copy about a message still on its way. The first option is the tempting one. This lesson shows why many systems allow this on purpose.

sections.h: Three copies of one balance, and what a read may return
sections.html:
Let's build the program behind that card. A small company runs a payments app. Each time someone pays a shop by card, it records who paid, which shop, how much and when, and it keeps a running balance for each account. Account acct-1001 holds 100.00. You pay 30.00, and the checkout, the part of the program that handles a payment at the till, writes the new balance: balance = 70.

With one copy, a read returns the last value written. But if that computer breaks, every balance goes with it. So the company keeps three copies, each on its own computer. A copy kept on another computer is a replica. One of them, the leader, takes every change first and sends it to the others, the followers, as a message over the network. The Replication track's lesson One leader, many followers built this setup.

Messages take time. Say the leader applies the write 10 ms (thousandths of a second) after the payment starts. Follower f1 applies it at 15 ms. Follower f2 runs on a busy computer and gets to it at 90 ms. A read at 20 ms gets 70 from the leader or f1, and the old 100 from f2. All three copies are healthy. They've reached different points in the same list of changes.

Couldn't f2 tell that it's behind? Not for sure. A message can be late or lost, and a copy can't tell "no new writes" from "the news hasn't arrived yet". Stamping each write with the time doesn't settle it either. Every computer has its own clock, and clocks drift apart by milliseconds or more, as the lesson Clocks you can't trust showed.

So is the 100 a bug? It depends on what the system promised. A consistency model is that promise, written down: a rule that says which values a read may return, given the writes around it. A strict rule saves your code work. A loose one leaves the work to you.

To check a promise, we describe only what the clients saw. A client is any program that sends requests to the copies, which together we'll call the store. The description is a history. Each request, called an operation, is a bar on a timeline, from when the request leaves the client to when the answer comes back. The store did the work at some instant inside the bar, and nobody outside knows exactly when. The figure shows two bars: checkout's write, and a read by the ledger, the program that keeps the account books.

A history shows two orders. In real-time order, if one bar ends before another begins, the first came first. In program order, each client (called a process here) runs one operation after another, so its own operations have an order too.

Here's the picture for the whole lesson. Every model asks one question: can we line up all the operations in one order that a single copy could have produced, while keeping some rule? "A single copy could have produced it" means each read returns the latest write before it in the line. Only the rule changes from model to model.

In the figure, the write ended at 10 ms and the read began at 20 ms. Keep real-time order, and the write comes first, so the read must say 70: the history fails. Keep only each process's own order, and the read may go first: it passes. The demo below runs a checker that asks it. Next, we'll walk down the models, one rule at a time.

try.title: Run the checker on five histories
steps: Open ModelsDemo.kt. It holds five small histories, written with the lab's history { } builder: a few lines of Kotlin that say which process read or wrote what, and from when to when, in ms. A read that returns - saw the value as it was before any write in the history, the old value.
Before you run it, guess for each history: could one copy have produced it, in the order the clock shows?

Run it from the labs folder. Each history gets six yes-or-no answers, one per model, strictest first; the next section explains them. For now, read the first answer, linearizable, and the order the checker found.
try.expect:
The first two histories (output trimmed to them):

one copy: every read sees the latest finished write
  checkout  w(balance,70)   0-10
  ledger    r(balance)=70  20-30
  linearizable yes  sequential yes  causal yes  read-your-writes yes  monotonic-reads yes  eventual yes
  one order that explains it: checkout w(balance,70), ledger r(balance)=70

stale: ledger starts after the write finished, and misses it
  checkout  w(balance,70)   0-10
  ledger    r(balance)=-   20-30
  linearizable no  sequential yes  causal yes  read-your-writes yes  monotonic-reads yes  eventual yes
  one order that explains it: ledger r(balance)=-, checkout w(balance,70)

The stale history fails linearizable, because real time puts the write first. It passes sequential, because the checker found an order with the ledger's read first, and that order breaks no process's own order. Each later history fails at least one more model. And eventual yes appears on every line: no history that ends can break eventual consistency, for a reason the next section gives.

sections.h: Down the ladder: six models, each one looser
sections.html:
Picture the models as rungs on a ladder. Each rung down drops one demand, so a history that passes a rung passes every rung below it.

The top rung is linearizable. The store behaves as if there were one copy, and each operation took effect at one instant inside its bar. Two things follow. A read that starts after a write has finished must see it. And once any read has returned the new value, every read that starts later must return it too, even while the write is still reaching some copies. The next lesson, Linearizability, is about this rung alone.

One rung down is sequential consistency, which Leslie Lamport defined in 1979. It drops real time but keeps one order that everybody agrees on, with each process's operations in the order the process ran them. A read can be stale, as in the figure. But two clients can never see two writes in opposite orders. The stepper's third frame shows that case.

Next is causal consistency, which drops the single order. Two writes are concurrent when neither could have known about the other. Causal consistency lets each process see concurrent writes in its own order, but never an effect before its cause. Cause means something exact here: an operation causes everything later in its own process, a write causes every read that returned its value, and these links chain. Say a support agent asks a shop a question in the app, and the shop reads it and answers. Nobody may see the answer and then fail to find the question. The lesson When followers lag called this consistent prefix reads.

Below causal sit the session guarantees: promises to one client about its own run of requests, its session. Douglas Terry and colleagues named four in 1994. Read your writes: after you write, your reads see it. Monotonic reads: once you've seen a value, you never see an older one. Monotonic writes: your writes take effect in the order you made them. Writes follow reads: a write you make after reading something is ordered after what you read. The lab checks the first two.

The bottom rung is eventual consistency: if the writes stop, all copies end up the same. It says nothing about what a read returns before then. A promise that something good happens in the end, with no deadline, is called a liveness promise, and no history that stops can break one. That's why eventual passes every frame of the stepper.

Why accept anything below the top? Because each rung up costs availability, the ability to keep answering while part of the network is cut off. Jepsen, a company that tests databases, publishes a map of these models that draws the line. When the network splits the copies into groups that can't reach each other, no model at or above sequential lets every copy keep answering: some must refuse. Causal and the session guarantees can be sticky available: a client that keeps talking to the same copy keeps working.

A stronger model is a promise someone pays for. Pick the loosest rung your data can live with. Next, we'll meet a word that sounds like linearizable and means something else.

The copies only agree once something settles the conflict, the subject of the Replication track's lesson Concurrent writes.

frames.say: Balance goes back. The ledger reads 70 from one copy, then the old value from a copy further behind. Monotonic reads says that once you've seen a value, you never see an older one. Eventual holds in all six frames: it only promises that copies agree once writes stop, and no history that stops can break that.

try.title: Write a history that is causal but not sequential
steps: Open ModelsDemo.kt and find mine(). Replace its body with a history of your own. Two rules: one process's bars may not overlap, because a process does one thing at a time, and each write to a key needs a new value.
Aim for causal yes and sequential no, without copying the "opposite orders" history. Hint: two processes are enough if each one also reads.
Run it with -Pargs=mine. If you get causal no, look for the cause and effect you broke.
try.expect:
One answer: two processes, eu and us, each write the status, then read back the other one's value.

fun mine(): History = history {
    "eu".write("status", 2, 0..10)
    "eu".read("status", 3, 20..30)
    "us".write("status", 3, 0..10)
    "us".read("status", 2, 20..30)
}

mine
  eu        w(status,2)     0-10   r(status)=3    20-30
  us        w(status,3)     0-10   r(status)=2    20-30
  linearizable no  sequential no  causal yes  read-your-writes yes  monotonic-reads yes  eventual yes

In any single order, one of the two writes comes last, and both reads after it would have to return that write. But each process on its own may put the other's write last, and no read depends on another, so causal holds. As shipped, mine() is the one-copy history, and every model says yes.

sections.h: Serializable and linearizable: two promises that sound alike
sections.html:
Two words look alike and get mixed up all the time: serializable and linearizable. Both say "as if in some single order". They answer different questions.

Serializable is about transactions. A transaction is a group of reads and writes that a database treats as one unit: all of it happens, or none of it. Moving 30.00 between two accounts is one: take it from the first, add it to the second. The Transactions track's lesson What a transaction promises defined serializable: the result is as if the transactions ran one at a time, in some order. Nothing says it must match the order in which they really happened. So a serializable database may answer a read-only transaction from an old snapshot, a frozen picture of the data at one moment. As long as the picture is consistent, the promise holds.

Linearizable is about one operation on one value, such as one balance, and it's all about recency: real time decides the order. It says nothing about a transaction that touches two rows, two records in a table. Picture two transfers that each check "the two accounts together hold at least 0" and then take money from a different account. Every single read and write can be linearizable, and the total can still go below zero. That's write skew, from the lesson Write skew and phantoms.

Put the two together, and you get strict serializable: transactions in one order, and that order respects real time. A transaction that starts after another has finished sees its effects. Spanner, a Google database spread over data centers (buildings full of computers) around the world, offers this and calls it external consistency. FoundationDB, a free database, offers it too. CockroachDB, a database built along Spanner's lines, offers serializable with some promises about recency, which falls short of strict. Oracle's SERIALIZABLE setting is really snapshot isolation, a weaker promise that allows write skew, so it doesn't even reach serializable.

The gap between serializable and strict serializable is easy to fall into once there are copies. Picture a ledger database that runs every write transaction on the leader, one at a time, so it's serializable by construction. To take load off the leader, read-only transactions run on a follower that applies changes 50 ms late. Checkout saves a payment at 30 ms. A ledger report starts at 60 ms on the follower and sees neither the new balance nor the payment. Both are missing together, so the picture is consistent, and the history is serializable: put the report before the payment. It isn't strict serializable, because the payment finished before the report began.

So ask two questions of each rule your data must keep. Does it span several rows? Then you need serializable transactions. Does a reader learn about a write some other way, and then expect to see it? Then you need linearizable, or strict serializable when the read covers several rows. Next, we'll cut the network and see what that forces.

try.title: A serializable database that returns old data
steps: Run SnapshotDemo. The leader runs write transactions one at a time. Read-only transactions read a consistent snapshot, first on a follower 50 ms behind, then on the leader. T1 to T4 are the four transactions, pay-7 is a payment, and captured means its money has moved.
Before you run it, predict what T3, the ledger's report, reads in each setup, and which setup is strict serializable.
Then run it with -Pargs=5 to put the follower only 5 ms behind. Does that make it strict serializable, or only less likely to show the problem?

read-only transactions on a follower (50 ms behind)
  T1 setup       0-5    writes balance=100
  T2 checkout   20-30   writes balance=70, pay-7=captured
  T3 ledger     60-70   reads  balance=100, pay-7=-
  T4 ledger    100-110  reads  balance=70, pay-7=captured
  serializable: yes, as T1, T3, T2, T4
  strict serializable (the order must also respect real time): no
  key balance on its own: linearizable no, sequential yes

read-only transactions on the leader

  T2 checkout   20-30   writes balance=70, pay-7=captured
  T3 ledger     60-70   reads  balance=70, pay-7=captured

On the follower, T3 sees the balance and the payment both missing: consistent, serializable as T1, T3, T2, T4, and out of date. On the leader, the same transactions are strict serializable. With a 5 ms lag, T3 happens to see everything, so this run is strict serializable too. But a T3 that starts 2 ms after T2 finishes would still miss it. A smaller lag shrinks the window and leaves the promise unchanged.

sections.h: When the network splits: what CAP proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
So far, slow copies have only made reads stale. Now let's cut the network. A partition is a break that splits the computers into groups that can't send messages to each other, while each group keeps running. A cut cable or a broken network box can cause one.

In 2000, the computer scientist Eric Brewer made a guess in a conference talk. A system that shares data across machines, he said, can have at most two of three things: consistency, availability and partition tolerance. He gave no exact definitions, which kept people arguing for years. The slogan "pick two of three" grew out of that talk, and it's wrong in a way worth understanding.

In 2002, Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch made it a theorem by pinning down each word. Consistency means linearizable, for one value you can read and write. Availability means every request that reaches a computer that hasn't failed gets an answer that isn't an error. A partition means the network may lose any number of messages. The theorem: in a network with no upper limit on how long a message may take, no system can promise both consistency and availability while messages can be lost.

The proof fits in a paragraph. Put one copy of the balance in Europe and one in the US, and cut the link between them. A payment arrives in Europe and takes 30.00 off the balance. A read arrives in the US. Availability says the US copy must answer. It has heard nothing from Europe, so it answers with the old balance. The write had finished before the read began, so linearizable is broken. To stay linearizable, the US copy must refuse or wait until the link comes back, and then it isn't available.

Now what the theorem doesn't say. You can't "pick" partition tolerance away: networks lose messages whether you choose it or not, as Partial failure, the first lesson of the Faults, time and truth track, showed. The honest reading is: while a partition lasts, a system either stays linearizable or keeps every copy answering. CAP says nothing about the long stretches with no partition, nothing about speed, and nothing about other models or other faults. And its availability is extreme: one refusing copy breaks it.

Martin Kleppmann, who wrote the book Designing Data-Intensive Applications, points out that a common setup is neither. A database with one leader and followers that lag isn't CAP-consistent, because reads from followers are stale. It isn't CAP-available either, because a client cut off from the leader can't write. It's still a useful system. Labels like "CP" (consistent when cut) and "AP" (available when cut) hide more than they tell.

Brewer came back to it in 2012. Partitions are rare, so a design should notice one, switch to a partition mode that limits what's allowed, and tidy up afterwards. His example is a cash machine that keeps paying out while it's cut off from the bank, but only up to a small limit, and settles the difference later. A card company that approves small payments when the bank can't be reached, and checks them afterwards, makes the same trade. Next, we'll see the price of consistency on a day when nothing is cut.

try.title: Answer or refuse while the network is cut
steps: Run CapDemo. It keeps three copies of one balance, in Europe (eu), the US (us) and Asia-Pacific (apac). From 1,000 ms to 3,000 ms, eu is cut off from both others. The same requests run twice: once where every copy answers from what it holds, and once where a request must first reach a majority, 2 of the 3 copies.
Before you run it, predict what checkout's write at 1,100 ms gets in each mode, and what the ledger's read at 1,200 ms returns.
Look at the times before the cut, too. Which mode pays on a healthy day?
try.expect:
available: every replica answers from its own copy
      0 ms  eu    checkout  writes balance=70  ok    after 1 ms
    100 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     70    after 1 ms
   1000 ms  eu is cut off from us and apac
   1100 ms  eu    checkout  writes balance=40  ok    after 1 ms
   1200 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     70    after 1 ms
   1300 ms  apac  fraud     writes balance=55  ok    after 1 ms
   3000 ms  the network heals
   3500 ms  eu    checkout  reads  balance     55    after 1 ms
   3500 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     55    after 1 ms
  the history of answered requests: linearizable no, eventual yes

consistent: a request must reach a majority (2 of 3 replicas) first
      0 ms  eu    checkout  writes balance=70  ok    after 81 ms (via us)
    100 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     70    after 81 ms (via eu)
   1000 ms  eu is cut off from us and apac
   1100 ms  eu    checkout  writes balance=40  refused after 500 ms: can't reach a majority
   1200 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     70    after 121 ms (via apac)
   1300 ms  apac  fraud     writes balance=55  ok    after 121 ms (via us)
   3000 ms  the network heals
   3500 ms  eu    checkout  reads  balance     55    after 81 ms (via us)
   3500 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     55    after 81 ms (via eu)
  the history of answered requests: linearizable yes, eventual yes

In available mode, eu accepts the 40 and us goes on saying 70: every copy answered, and the history isn't linearizable. When the network heals, the copies keep the write with the latest time on it, a rule called last write wins, and that's apac's 55. Checkout's 40 vanished without an error. (With real clocks that drift, "latest" isn't even reliable.) In consistent mode, eu refuses for the whole cut while us and apac carry on, and the history is linearizable. Notice the healthy-day cost: 81 ms instead of 1 ms for every request, because each one waits for a round trip to a second copy. CAP doesn't mention it. The next section does.

aside.title: Why wait for a majority, and not for every copy?
aside.html: If every write waited for all three copies, one broken computer would stop every write, and the copies were there to survive exactly that. If a write waited for one copy, it could vanish with that copy. A majority sits between the two: with three copies it's two, so one copy can fail and writes go on. And any two majorities of the same three copies share at least one copy. So a request that reaches a majority always meets a copy that took part in the last write that reached a majority. That shared copy is the idea under almost everything in this track, including the agreement protocols of lesson 3.

sections.h: Paying for consistency on a quiet day: PACELC and the settings that choose
sections.html:
The CAP demo's consistent mode paid about 80 ms on every request, with no partition anywhere. That cost is with you every day. Latency is the time a request waits for its answer. Daniel Abadi's PACELC (2012, said "pass-elk") names the trade: if there's a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. A store that waits for other copies before it answers is consistent and slow. One that answers from the nearest copy is fast and may be stale. Inside one data center, the wait is a millisecond or two. Between distant regions it's a round trip, the time for a message to go there and back: about 70 ms between the east coast of the US and Europe.

Most stores today let you choose for each request, and the table maps a few settings to what each buys. Cassandra is a free database that keeps copies with no single leader. DynamoDB is a database service that Amazon runs. MongoDB keeps one leader, which it calls the primary, and followers called secondaries. A failover is when the primary fails and a secondary takes over.

Store and setting What it waits for What a client gets
Cassandra 5.0, ONE one copy answers eventual: you can miss your own write
Cassandra 5.0, QUORUM (3 copies) 2 of 3 copies, on each write and each read, so the two groups overlap every read meets every finished write, but the latest timestamp wins, and the next lesson shows it still isn't linearizable
DynamoDB, default read any copy answers eventual: may miss a write that just succeeded
DynamoDB, ConsistentRead=true the read reflects every write that succeeded before it up-to-date reads in one region, at twice the read cost
MongoDB 9.0, default (readConcern: "local") writes wait for a majority; a read takes the copy's newest data a read can return data that a failover later undoes
MongoDB 9.0, readConcern: "majority" a read takes only what a majority holds never undone, but can be stale
MongoDB 9.0, readConcern: "linearizable" the primary checks with a majority that it's still primary linearizable, for one document (one record)

Read the table as three questions you can ask of any store. How many copies must hold a write before you hear OK? Which copy, or how many, may answer a read? Does the copy that answers check that it's still allowed to, that it's still the leader and holds the latest write? Each extra "yes" moves you up the ladder and costs waiting, which is PACELC's E.

Two traps. Defaults usually sit below linearizable: MongoDB's default read can return a write that a failover then undoes, and DynamoDB's default read can miss a write that just succeeded. And a setting buys a model only for the operations that use it. A QUORUM write paired with a ONE read gives you ONE.

The ladder has a limit, too. It describes what a read may see. No rung on it stops two clients who both read "seat free" from both writing "mine". For that, the copies must agree on one decision, and that's where this track is heading.

try.title: Time PACELC on three MongoDB copies
steps: MongoDB is a popular database program, and a group of its copies with one primary is called a replica set. From the labs folder, start a set of three with docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml up -d --wait. Docker runs each copy in its own container, a sealed box on your laptop. It takes about 30 seconds and about 1.5 GB of Docker's memory.

Run the commands below. First they time w: 1 (wait for the primary only) against w: "majority" (wait for 2 of 3) on a healthy set. Then db.fsyncLock() makes both secondaries stop applying writes, as if the primary were cut off from them, and the same write and three reads run with a 2-second limit.
Predict before you run: which write fails, and what do the local, majority and linearizable reads return?
The last command stops the set and deletes its data.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.html: # a healthy set: time each write concern three times docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval ' db.balances.insertOne({_id: "acct-1001", balanceMinor: 10000}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority"}}); for (const w of [1, "majority", 1, "majority", 1, "majority"]) { const t = Date.now(); db.balances.updateOne({_id: "acct-1001"}, {$inc: {balanceMinor: -100}}, {writeConcern: {w}}); print("w:" + w, Date.now() - t, "ms"); }' # both secondaries stop applying replication: the primary is as good as cut off for m in mongo2 mongo3; do docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec $m mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.fsyncLock().ok'; done # the same write and three reads, each with a 2-second limit docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval ' for (const w of [1, "majority"]) { const t = Date.now(); try { db.balances.updateOne({_id: "acct-1001"}, {$inc: {balanceMinor: -2500}}, {writeConcern: {w, wtimeout: 2000}}); print("w:" + w, "ok", Date.now() - t, "ms") } catch (e) { print("w:" + w, e.codeName, Date.now() - t, "ms") } } for (const level of ["local", "majority", "linearizable"]) { const t = Date.now(); try { const d = db.balances.find({_id: "acct-1001"}).readConcern(level).maxTimeMS(2000).next(); print(level, d.balanceMinor, Date.now() - t, "ms") } catch (e) { print(level, e.codeName, Date.now() - t, "ms") } }' for m in mongo2 mongo3; do docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec $m mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.fsyncUnlock().ok'; done docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml down -v

On a healthy set, waiting for a majority cost 1 to 3 ms more than w: 1. Here the copies are containers on one laptop; between regions, the wait would be a round trip. That's the E in PACELC. With the secondaries frozen, w: 1 still answered (available, and at risk of being undone later), while w: "majority" gave up after 2 seconds: the P choice, made for each write. The reads split the same way. local returned 4400 (44.00, since amounts are in cents), which includes two withdrawals that no secondary holds. majority returned 9400, the last value a majority holds. linearizable refused, because the primary couldn't confirm with a majority that it was still primary. The timed-out write wasn't undone on the primary, which is why local shows it. Your timings will differ, so compare the pairs.

refs.title: Abadi, Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design (PDF)

mistake: Reading "strongly consistent" on a product's page as one well-known promise. People take it to mean linearizable for every operation, and build a check such as "is this username taken?" on top. Then they find that the promise covered only some reads (DynamoDB's strongly consistent reads skip its extra lookup tables, called global secondary indexes), only some settings (MongoDB's linearizable read needs w: "majority" and a query that matches one document), or only one key. It's an easy mistake, because the phrase is vague and every company uses it. The fix: write down the model, the operations and the settings ("linearizable reads of one document, with readConcern: linearizable and w: majority"), and test the claim with a history checker like this lesson's lab before you rely on it.
opening:
You share a card with your sister. You pay 30.00 for coffee, and the app on your phone shows 70.00 left. You text her to check. A moment later her app shows 100.00, as if you'd never paid. She refreshes: 70.00.

Nothing is broken. The company keeps each balance on three computers, so that losing one loses nothing. Your payment reached one copy first, and her phone asked one that hadn't heard yet.

It's tempting to say the copies should always agree. On one computer they do, because a read returns the last value written, as with every variable in a program. With three copies, "the last value" depends on which copy you ask, and when.

In Testing distributed systems, we judged a system by its history: what its clients asked and were told. To call a history wrong, we need a rule for a right one. In this lesson, we'll write those rules down, test small histories against them, and see what keeping copies in step costs. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a shared card that said 70.00 on your phone and 100.00 on your sister's. That history breaks the top rung, linearizable, and keeps every rung below it. A store that promised only those did nothing wrong.

Next time an app shows a number that many people change, such as seats left on a flight, open it on two devices and refresh both at once. If they disagree for a moment, you've found an app that chose a lower rung.

Next, we'll climb to the top rung. What exactly does "behave like one copy" demand, how do you check a history against it, and why doesn't waiting for 2 of 3 copies give it?

compare.title: The same balance read, two promises

a.label: MongoDB, default
a.title: fast, may be undone
a.html: val balances = db.getCollection("balances") // w: majority is the default since 5.0; reads use readConcern local val doc = balances.find(eq("_id", "acct-1001")).first() // newest data on the node you hit, including writes a failover can roll back

b.label: MongoDB, linearizable
b.title: slower, one document, primary only
b.html: val strict = db.getCollection("balances") .withReadPreference(ReadPreference.primary()) .withReadConcern(ReadConcern.LINEARIZABLE) .withWriteConcern(WriteConcern.MAJORITY) val doc = strict.find(eq("_id", "acct-1001")).maxTime(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS).first() // sees every majority write that finished before the read began

compare.note: The left read answers from whichever copy it reaches, with that copy's newest data. The right read must go to the primary, which first checks with a majority that it's still the primary. That costs a round trip, and it can wait during an election, while the copies choose a new primary, so the code sets a time limit. It's linearizable only for a query that matches one document, MongoDB's word for one record.

worked.title: Name the model a refund really gets

steps.say: Start from the rule the data must keep, in words. A refund may be given only if the payment's money has moved (its status is captured) and it hasn't been refunded already. Two refund requests for one payment must not both pass. Then list who reads and who writes.
steps.code:
invariant: at most one refund per captured payment
readers:   refund-service (decides), merchant dashboard (shows)
writers:   capture-service, refund-service

steps.say: Find the write setting. Here the refund is written to Cassandra 5.0, a database that keeps copies with no single leader, at QUORUM: 2 of the 3 copies must store it.
steps.code: val write = SimpleStatement.newInstance( "UPDATE payments SET status = 'refunded' WHERE payment_id = ?", paymentId) .setConsistencyLevel(DefaultConsistencyLevel.QUORUM)

steps.say: Find the read setting. The refund check reads at QUORUM too, so it overlaps every finished write. Yet two refund checks that run at the same moment can both see captured and both write refunded. Each one checked and then acted, and the other acted in between. That's a race, and no read model fixes it.
steps.code: val check = SimpleStatement.newInstance( "SELECT status FROM payments WHERE payment_id = ?", paymentId) .setConsistencyLevel(DefaultConsistencyLevel.QUORUM)

steps.say: Pick the loosest model that keeps the rule. "At most one" needs a linearizable compare-and-set on one row: change the status only if it still says captured. Cassandra offers this as a lightweight transaction, which runs Paxos, an agreement protocol and the subject of lesson 3. The shop's screen can keep reading at ONE.
steps.code: val refund = SimpleStatement.newInstance( "UPDATE payments SET status = 'refunded' WHERE payment_id = ? IF status = 'captured'", paymentId) .setSerialConsistencyLevel(DefaultConsistencyLevel.SERIAL) val applied = session.execute(refund).wasApplied() // false: someone else refunded it first

steps.say: Write the result down next to the code, so the next person doesn't have to work it out again. LWT is short for lightweight transaction.
steps.code:
refund decision: linearizable CAS (LWT, SERIAL)   several round trips per write
refund display:  eventual (ONE)                   may lag by seconds

lab.title: A checker for consistency models
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder with the command above. They need no Docker and run in about a second. All 15 fail, because the functions they test are still TODO. Read History.kt first. Op is one operation: who did it, what it did, from when to when, and the result. The history { } builder writes a history in a few lines. Search.legalOrder finds an order in which every read returns the latest write before it, and which keeps a mustPrecede rule you pass in.
Exercise 1: write realTime(a, b) (a ended before b started) and programOrder(a, b) (same process, a first). Each is one line.

Exercise 2: write causalOrder(h). Start from program order. Add a link from each write to every read that returned its value (h.writeOf(read)). Then add every link you can reach by chaining links, which is called closing it under transitivity. For histories this small, a true-or-false grid and three nested loops are plenty.

Exercise 3: write satisfies(h, model). Linearizable and sequential are one Search.exists over all operations each. Causal and the two session guarantees are one search per process, over all writes plus that process's own operations, each with its own rule. Eventual is true.

Run the tests until all pass. ModelsTest holds the stepper's histories. LadderPropertyTest checks 300 histories made by one copy that applies each operation at once (every model must hold) and 300 random ones (a stronger model must always imply the looser ones).
hints: Read your writes, for a process p: a must come before b when both are p's, a is a write, b is a read and a came first. Monotonic reads: both are p's reads, and a came first.

Causal, per process: use the rule from causalOrder(h) as it is. Links that pass through other processes' reads are already in it, because you chained links over the whole history before narrowing the search to one process's view.

If the property test fails, jqwik, the library that makes the random histories, prints the seed, and your assertion message includes the history. Paste it into a plain test with the history { } builder and print classify(h).

drill.title: Each model in one line
drill.prompt: Without looking, write satisfies(h, model) for all six models, given Search.exists(ops, mustPrecede), realTime, programOrder and causalOrder(h). For the models that check one process at a time, say which operations go into each search.

answer.html: fun satisfies(h: History, model: Model): Boolean { fun view(p: String) = h.ops.filter { it.kind == Kind.WRITE || it.process == p } return when (model) { Model.LINEARIZABLE -> Search.exists(h.ops, ::realTime) Model.SEQUENTIAL -> Search.exists(h.ops, ::programOrder) Model.CAUSAL -> causalOrder(h).let { before -> h.processes.all { Search.exists(view(it), before) } } Model.READ_YOUR_WRITES -> h.processes.all { p -> Search.exists(view(p)) { a, b -> a.process == p && b.process == p && a.kind == Kind.WRITE && b.kind == Kind.READ && programOrder(a, b) } } Model.MONOTONIC_READS -> h.processes.all { p -> Search.exists(view(p)) { a, b -> a.process == p && b.process == p && a.kind == Kind.READ && b.kind == Kind.READ && programOrder(a, b) } } Model.EVENTUAL -> true } }

recap: A consistency model is a promise about which values a read may return. Each model asks whether the operations can be lined up in one order that a single copy could have produced, while keeping some rule. Only the rule changes.

Strictest to loosest: linearizable keeps real time; sequential keeps each process's own order; causal never shows an effect before its cause; the session guarantees (read your writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes follow reads) cover one client's own session; eventual only promises that the copies end up the same.
Serializable is about transactions over many rows, in some order, and allows stale reads. Linearizable is about one value and recency, and allows write skew. Strict serializable is both at once.

CAP, as Gilbert and Lynch proved it: when messages can be lost, no system can be linearizable and keep every copy answering. It covers one model and one fault. PACELC adds the cost you pay with no fault at all: waiting.

Stores let you choose for each request (Cassandra's levels, DynamoDB's ConsistentRead, MongoDB's read concern), and the defaults usually sit below linearizable. A strong write paired with a weak read gets the weak read's promise.

The limit: these models describe what a read may see. None of them stops two clients who both read "free" from both writing "mine". That takes copies that agree on one decision, which is where this track is heading.

explain.prompt: The café owner asks you why the shop's screen in the payments app sometimes shows a refund that the app's main page says hasn't happened yet, when the company's website says its database is "strongly consistent". Explain it to her in plain words.
explain.answer: The database keeps several copies of every record, and each copy hears about a change a few milliseconds after the others. "Strongly consistent" on the website only covers certain reads, made with certain settings. The main page reads with the setting that waits for the latest copy, so it shows exactly what has been saved. The shop's screen uses the fast default, which answers from whichever copy is nearest. Right after a change, that copy can be ahead of or behind the one the main page used. Here the screen's copy got the refund first, or the main page was asked a moment before the refund was saved. Both answers are allowed by the promises the app chose. If the screen must never contradict the main page, it has to use the slower setting too, and every page load will wait a little longer. For a screen, a short disagreement is usually fine. For the decision to give a refund, it isn't, which is why that part of the app uses the strict setting.

deeper.html:
Jepsen's map. Jepsen's map of consistency models puts this lesson's models and the transaction levels from the Transactions track on one picture, joined at strict serializable, and colours each one by how available it can be during a partition. It's the best one-page reference on the subject. The availability classes come from work by Peter Bailis and colleagues on highly available transactions, which showed that some models, such as read committed (a level from the Transactions track) and the session guarantees, can be served without waiting on other copies.

Fifty models, two relations. Paolo Viotti and Marko Vukolić's survey defines more than 50 consistency models exactly, for single values without transactions, and orders them by strength. Their trick is to describe each model with two relations: visibility (which writes a read can see) and arbitration (one overall order that settles conflicts).

Abadi's labels. In the PACELC paper, Abadi labelled systems by their defaults: Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak as PA/EL, BigTable and HBase as PC/EC, and the MongoDB of 2012 as PA/EC. Read those as descriptions of default settings, since every modern store lets you change them.

More settings, more rungs. The section's table left some settings out. Cassandra 5.0's IF NOT EXISTS with SERIAL runs a round of Paxos (lesson 3) for the rows under one key, and gives a linearizable compare-and-set there. MongoDB 9.0's causally consistent sessions, with majority reads and writes, carry a marker of the newest change the session has seen, and give causal consistency plus the session guarantees. PostgreSQL 18's synchronous_commit = remote_apply makes a commit wait until the synchronous standby (PostgreSQL's word for a follower) has applied it, which gives read your writes when you read that standby. Kafka 4.4's acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 sets how many copies hold a record before the program that wrote it hears OK, and readers only see records that every up-to-date copy holds; the Messaging track has the details. And DynamoDB's ConsistentRead doesn't apply to global secondary indexes, its extra lookup tables.

Checking fast. The lab's checker treats each model as a search for an order, which can take very long in the worst case. Real tools avoid that for transactions. Jepsen's Elle works out which transaction depended on which from the values they read, and looks for cycles (A depended on B, and B on A), which takes time roughly in step with the history's length. The next lesson builds the search for linearizable properly.

Further reading. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 10, covers consistency models and CAP from the angle of replicated databases.
